newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-ELS HAS WHAT MONTGOMERIE NEEDS - COMPOSURE, OPEN TITLE.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-ELS HAS WHAT MONTGOMERIE NEEDS - COMPOSURE, OPEN TITLE.

text.p: Ernie Els has it and Colin Montgomerie needs it.

Composure is what separated the two great golfers at the end. That is what kept Montgomerie from hoisting the trophy he dearly covets, the one that belonged to Els after their draining duel on Sunday at Congressional.
Tom Lehman was also there at the end. Like Montgomerie, Lehman was unable to beat back the doubts, leaving the mellow Mr. Els to scoop up his second U.S. Open in four years.
"I think with experience you become a little bit more calm," said Els, the serene South African. "You have to be calm to win major tournaments."

Els even kept tabs on the scoreboard, a lesson he learned in winning the 1994 Open at Oakmont, where he had to engage in a three-way playoff that included Montgomerie after mistakenly thinking he needed to birdie the 72nd hole to win in regulation when only par was needed.
"Ernie was frightfully calm out there and that's what you need to win this tournament. His nature helps him in these situations," said Montgomerie, who played with Els on Sunday.
The Briton, increasingly concerned he may be deeded the permanent title of best player not to win a major, revealed as much about himself as his conqueror with that comment.

In a championship he lost by one stroke, Montgomerie blustered and got flustered in Friday's weather-interrupted second round and shot a 76 that cost him precious ground. He argued with louts and innocuous fans alike in the gallery.

Sunday, Montgomerie waited on the 17th green for about five minutes for a commotion in the galleries on a hillside above the green to subside. Annoyed by the delay, he finally stepped up to his crucial five-foot par putt and missed.
"It's getting me down now, this major business," the pudgy 33-year-old Scot said, admitting the pressure to succeed grows with each lost opportunity.
"I cried after the round, sure," said Montgomerie, who also lost a playoff at the 1995 PGA Championship. "I'm only human in saying that."
Lehman had pain of his own to deal with.

The reigning British Open champion fired at the flags in hopes of catching Els at the end but saw his last chance splash into the water guarding 17. He has led going to the final round of the U.S. Open three years in a row without cashing in.

"You just don't have many great chances unless you're a phenomenal, phenomenal player," said Lehman, last year's U.S. Player of the Year. "I've had a lot of chances and Monty has had a lot of chances. I've only won one. He hasn't won any.
"The part that really hurts is knowing that I'm still lacking something, I guess, to just get the job done. And Monte maybe is feeling the same thing."
The 97th Open was more than just a tale of two losers, however compelling.
It provided a reminder that there is more than one immensely talented 20-something golf sensation in the universe.
Els, who finished at four-under-par 276, showed yet again his flowing swing, smooth power and accomplished short game form an irresistable triple threat at the majors.

All the attention heaped on 21-year-old Masters champion Tiger Woods, who finished 10 shots back, and all the delays and early morning re-starts in this storm-plagued event deflected focus from the estimable Els.
All Els has done since 1992, when he was 22, is produce nine top 10 finishes in the majors -- including six in the top five and, of course, two U.S. Open titles.
"I always knew I had something special," Els told a television interviewer. "Major championship golf is such a major challenge. You have to dig so much deeper."
Els eyed the example of the greatest major championship player -- Jack Nicklaus, the winner of 18 major titles, who competed in his 150th major championship last week at Congressional.
"If you look at Jack Nicklaus, you know, he made it happen," Els said. "And he was calm. He was always in control of his game. And it's hard to do that. But I'm getting closer."
